links.note: 141 says the folly (பேதைமை) of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found (இல்) in those who have seen aram and porul; 910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is never found (இல்) in those with a deliberating mind. Both end on 'பேதைமை ... இல்' and treat the lapse as a failure of understanding that knowledge excludes, once about another's wife in the Book of Virtue and once about subservience to one's own in the Book of Wealth.

832 defines the folly of all follies (பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை) as setting one's love on what is not proper to one (கையல்லதன்கண் காதன்மை). 141 names one case of exactly that: the பேதைமை of desiring (பெட்டு ஒழுகும்) a woman who is another's. Read together, 141 is an instance of the general definition that 832 gives much later.

142 says that among all who stand outside virtue (அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம்) none is a greater fool than the one who stands at another's door (பிறன்கடை); 150 says that even one who does not keep to virtue and does wrong (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) does well not to desire another's woman. Both verses rank within the class of the non-virtuous, and both put this one offence at the bottom, 142 by naming the worst case and 150 by naming the one abstention still worth having.

143 says those who go on doing evil in the home of people who trust them (தெளிந்தாரில்) are 'no different from the dead' (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 926 uses the same construction for sleepers (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்) and extends it to drinkers. Parimelazhagar explains 926 by the absence of awareness and 143 by the loss of aram, porul and inbam, so the same formula of living death is applied to a moral failure in one verse and to loss of consciousness in the other.

143 counts the betrayer of a trusting household as no different from the dead (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 214 says only the one who knows what is fitting lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). In both, being alive is measured by conduct and not by breath, once for a wrong committed and once for a duty to others left undone.

144 asks what greatness comes to, however great a person is (எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம்), if he enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). 965 says even those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) sink if they do a lowering deed as small as a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not outweigh a degrading act; 965 gives the general rule and 144 one named act.

Both verses use the millet's measure (தினைத்துணை). In 433 those who are ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a fault of a millet's size as large as a palmyra; in 144 the man entering another's home does not reflect even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). The pair shows the same measure from opposite sides: the careful person enlarges the smallest fault, and the adulterer does not give the smallest thought.

145 says one who crosses into another's home thinking it easy (எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான்) gets blame that stands forever without dying (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). 284 says a love grown strong in theft (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்) yields at harvest a distress that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). The same logic, a desire for what is another's that looks light at the start and has a permanent result, is applied to another's wife and to another's goods.

233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands without perishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்). 145 says the blame of the man who violates another's home also stands forever without dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Taken literally 145 names a second undying thing, so the pair shows the book treating lasting blame as the counterpart of lasting fame.

146 lists four things that never leave the man who crosses into another's home: enmity, sin, fear and blame (பகை பாவம் அச்சம் பழி). 171 says that one who covets another's good property without fairness finds his family ruined and fault brought on at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). Coveting another's wife and coveting another's goods are both given immediate, compound consequences; Parimelazhagar reads the பழி of 146 as blame on the family (குடிப்பழி), which brings it closer to the குடி of 171.

Both verses use the formula 'the one called a householder' (இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான்). 41 defines him by what he supports: he is the steady help of the three on their good path. 147 defines him by what he refrains from: he lives the household life with aram (அறனியலான்) who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another (பிறனியலாள் பெண்மை நயவாதவன்). Together they give a positive and a negative test for the same title.

49 says that what is called aram is household life, and that it is good if there is nothing in it that another blames (பிறன்பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). 147 says the householder living by aram is the one who does not desire another's woman. 147 can be read as naming a specific condition under which the household life of 49 stays free of others' blame; chapter 15 itself (145, 146) names பழி as the result of the offence.

Both verses redefine பேராண்மை, great manliness. 773 says people call fierceness (தறுகண்) great manliness, and that help given when something befalls the foe (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 148 gives the name to not looking at another's wife (பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை). In both, the word for martial valour is moved toward restraint; Parimelazhagar on 148 says it is called 'great' because the inner enemy, desire, is harder to subdue than outer enemies.

1026 says what is called good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself able to govern the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை); 148 calls not looking at another man's home or wife (பிறன்மனை) great manliness (பேராண்மை). Both locate ஆண்மை in the household and not on the battlefield: one in building up one's own house, the other in leaving another's alone.

148 praises not even looking at (நோக்காத) another's wife; Parimelazhagar glosses this as not taking her into the mind. 282 says that even thinking in the heart (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods (பிறன்பொருளை) by stealth is wrong. In both chapters the prohibition is moved back from the act to the look or the thought, for another's wife and for another's property.

149 says those entitled to good (நலக்குரியார்) are those who do not touch the shoulders of a woman who belongs to another (பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள் தோயாதார்). 916 says those who would spread their own good (தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார்) do not touch (தோயார்) the shoulders of women who spread a base charm to all. The same phrase for sexual union, தோள் தோய்தல், and the same word நலம் are used for the two forbidden unions, with another's wife and with courtesans, and in both abstaining is tied to one's own நலம்.

The two verses share a construction. 150: even if one does not keep to aram and does what is not aram (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is good not to desire another's woman. 181: even if one does not speak of aram and does what is not aram (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is pleasing to be called one who does not backbite. Each chapter picks out its own abstention as the one that still counts for a person who otherwise fails at virtue.

150 says not desiring another's woman is good even in one who practises no aram and does wrong; 297 says that if one can keep to not lying, then not doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை) is still good. Both isolate a single restraint and say it holds its value without the rest of virtue. Set side by side, the book makes this kind of claim for more than one virtue, so each is better read as emphasis than as a ranking.

151 holds up the earth that supports those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்) as the model for bearing with those who scorn us. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for aram that the earth bears the weight (வையம் ... பொறை) of the man who watches for someone's absence and speaks mean words. Both make the earth the bearer of people who abuse; 151 offers it as an example to follow, and 189 uses it to express wonder that the slanderer is tolerated at all.

In 151 the earth holds up (தாங்கும்) even those who dig into it. In 990, if the worthy decline in their worthiness, the great earth itself will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). The earth's bearing, which 151 treats as unconditional toward those who injure it, is in 990 made to depend on the character of the சான்றோர், and the word பொறை, burden, is the same word that names the forbearance of chapter 16.

151 says bearing with those who scorn us is the foremost thing (பொறுத்தல் தலை). 579, in the chapter on kindly regard in the Book of Wealth, says that showing regard and bearing (கண்ணோடிப் பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை) even with those whose nature is to hurt us is the foremost quality. The same ranking, with the same words பொறுத்தல் and தலை, is given for the householder and again for the ruler.

152 says to bear excess always, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 108 says it is not good to forget a good done, and that it is good to forget what is not good that very day (நன்றல்லது அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று). Both end on forgetting a wrong as the good thing; 108 adds the contrast that kindness must not be forgotten and specifies 'that very day', which Parimelazhagar also reads into 152 (அப்பொழுதே மறத்தல்).

Parimelazhagar reads 152 as telling one to bear a wrong even when one is able to punish it (தாம் ஒறுத்தற்கு இயன்ற காலத்தும்). 301 states that condition outright: only the one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back, and where it cannot, it makes no difference. 301 supplies the reason the commentator's condition matters: forbearance toward those one cannot hurt is not yet forbearance.

152 says to bear transgression always (என்றும்) and better still to forget it. 488, advising a king on timing, says: on seeing enemies, bear them (சுமக்க); when their end is seen to have come, the head goes down (கிழக்காம் தலை). In 488 the bearing is temporary and is kept in mind until the moment to act, where 152 asks for a bearing with no end that passes into forgetting. The Book of Wealth thus limits to a tactic what the Book of Virtue states without condition.

153 says the poverty within poverty is turning away a guest (இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால்); 89 says the poverty within having (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) is the folly of not tending guests, found in fools (மடவார்). The two share the paradox of a 'poverty' that is really inhospitality, and the word மடவார்: in 89 the fools are those who neglect guests, and in 153 they are the people one must bear with.

Both verses name a 'poverty within poverty' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and give different answers: in 153 it is turning away a guest, in 841 it is lack of understanding (அறிவின்மை), with other lack not counted as lack by the world. The same superlative formula serves hospitality in the Book of Virtue and intelligence in the Book of Wealth, which shows the formula working as emphasis within each chapter's topic.

153 says the strength within strength (வன்மையுள் வன்மை) is bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை); 444 says the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is to live so that those greater than oneself become one's own. Neither verse puts strength in force. One finds it in enduring those below one in understanding and the other in attaching oneself to those above.

154 says that one who wants நிறையுடைமை never to leave should guard forbearance; Parimelazhagar glosses நிறை here as சால்பு. 987 asks what use சால்பு is if one does not do pleasing things even to those who have done one harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two say the same thing from both ends: forbearance keeps சால்பு in place, and சால்பு that does not show in the treatment of offenders is worth nothing.

154 ties நிறை to forbearance: to keep நிறையுடைமை, live guarding பொறையுடைமை. 864 pairs the same two things in the negative, describing the man who does not leave off anger and has no நிறை (நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன்) as easy prey for anyone. The commentators gloss நிறை differently in the two places (Parimelazhagar: சால்பு in 154; Pope, following him, has keeping secrets in 864; Manakkudavar on 154 has a conduct of self-guarding), but in both verses its presence goes with restraint of anger and its absence with unchecked anger.

155 says the wise do not count as anything those who punish in return (ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையார்) and keep those who forbear like stored gold. 314 keeps the word ஒறுத்தல் and gives it a new content: the way to punish those who have done harm is to shame them by doing them good (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 thus shows the only form of 'punishing' that 155's judgment leaves open. (The Parimelazhagar text displayed for 314 in this edition belongs to 315.)

155 says those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்) are not counted as anything. 549 says that guarding the people and removing wrongdoing (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain on a king but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar restricts 155 to a harm done to oneself, and 549 concerns a ruler acting for his subjects, so 549 marks the limit of 155: the low regard for punishing applies to personal retaliation and not to the office of justice.

156 sets the one day's joy of those who retaliate (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்) against the lasting renown of those who forbear. 173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not aram out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). Both argue against a wrong by the shortness of the pleasure it buys, for retaliation in one verse and for coveting in the other.

156 grants the retaliator one day's pleasure and gives the forbearing renown to the end. 856 says that the life of one who says it is sweet (இனிது) to prevail in hostility is close to failure and ruin (தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து). Both admit that getting the better of an opponent tastes sweet and both say the sweetness is brief; the verse in the Book of Wealth names ruin where the verse in the Book of Virtue names only the loss of lasting fame.

156 says those who forbear have renown until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்), against one day's pleasure for those who retaliate; 145 says the man who violates another's home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). The adjacent chapters use the same accounting, a brief gratification weighed against a permanent reputation, with புகழ் on one side and பழி on the other. Manakkudavar takes பொன்றுந் துணையும் as until the person's own death, Parimelazhagar as until the world ends.

157 says that though others do what is improper to one (திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும்), it is good not to do what is not aram. 312 says that even when someone has done harm out of hatred, not doing harm in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the settled principle of the stainless. The same rule appears in the householder's chapter on forbearance and in the ascetic's chapter on not harming, which makes it common to both ways of life.

157: though others do one wrong, not doing what is not aram is good (அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). 852: though someone does unbearable things intending division (பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), not doing harm with hostility in mind is the chief thing (இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). The 'even if they do ... not doing' structure and the refusal to answer in kind recur in the Book of Wealth's chapter on hostility, where the reason given is political prudence as well as virtue.

Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read நோநொந்து in 157 as grieving for the suffering that will come to the wrongdoers. 319 states the mechanism behind that expectation: if one does harm to others in the forenoon, harm comes to oneself in the afternoon of its own accord (தாமே வரும்). On the commentators' reading 157 presupposes 319: the injured person pities the offender because the offence will return on him, and for the same reason does not add a wrong of his own. Kalaignar instead takes the pain in 157 as the injured person's own.

158 says to overcome those who do excessive wrong out of arrogance (மிகுதியான்) by one's own worthiness (தகுதியான் வென்றுவிடல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as forbearance. 985 says the strength of the able is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both describe yielding as the means of prevailing and use the vocabulary of contest, வெல்லல் and படை, for it.

158 calls forbearance toward the arrogant a victory (வென்றுவிடல்). 986 says the touchstone of சால்பு is to accept defeat (தோல்வி ... கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equals. The same conduct toward an overbearing lesser person is named winning in one verse and taking a loss in the other; 986 adds that it has to be felt and accepted as a defeat, which guards against reading 158 as a way of scoring over the offender. Manakkudavar on 158 says explicitly that forbearing is not defeat but is itself the victory.

158 says one defeats the overbearing by one's own forbearing worth. 1327, spoken by the man in the Book of Love, says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as is seen in the union that follows. The paradox that giving way is the real victory appears in ethics and again, in a dramatised speech, in love; the second is a lover's remark and not a moral rule, but the shape of the thought is the same.

Both verses play on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார். 310: those who go beyond bounds in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). 159: those who endure harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல்) have the purity of renouncers (துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை). In both, a householder's control over anger, his own or his response to another's, earns the standing of renunciation.

159 says those who endure (நோற்கிற்பவர்) the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from aram has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both apply the ascetic's verb நோல் to the householder and set him level with or above the ascetic; Parimelazhagar on 159 adds that these are people who remain in household life.

159 praises those who endure harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல்) from people who overstep. 389 says the world rests under the parasol of the king who has the character to bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). The same capacity is a private virtue in one verse and a quality of rule in the other. Parimelazhagar takes the bitter words of 389 to be the rebukes of advisers, so there the speaker means well, unlike the transgressors of 159.

The two verses have the same build. 160: those who endure without eating (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but behind those who endure others' harsh words (நோற்பாரின் பின்). 225: the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and it comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Each grants the faster his greatness and then places a household virtue, forbearance in one and giving in the other, ahead of him with the same closing word பின்.

261 defines the form of tavam as two things: bearing the pain that comes to one (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) and doing no harm to living beings. 160 uses the same verb for both the faster and the one who endures harsh words (நோற்பார்). By 261's definition the person in 160 who bears abuse and does not retaliate already meets both parts of tavam, which explains how 160 can rank him ahead of those who fast.

160 ranks those who fast behind those who bear harsh words; 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). In both a virtue of everyday speech, enduring it in one case and keeping it truthful in the other, is placed above formal religious practice.
